summary: Xaosseed's blog post for the February 2024 RPG Blog Carnival on illusions and delusions, hosted by Illusory Sensorum, examines how illusions disrupt the TTRPG gameplay loop. It draws on Blue Bard's articles on illusion save mechanics, johnbragg's internal/external illusion idea from RPG.net, and a taxonomy of illusionist aims (hide or fake hazards, delay characters, hide or fake boons), then proposes a passive vs active illusion split. The author concludes illusions should be used sparingly because their key advantage is surprise.
one_line: A February 2024 RPG Blog Carnival post on balancing illusions against the TTRPG gameplay loop, with a passive/active illusion framework.
key_facts: The post was published on 21 February 2024 as part of the RPG Blog Carnival on the topic of Illusions & Delusions.
The blog carnival was hosted by Illusory Sensorum for the topic of Illusions & Delusions.
The author says illusions mess with the core gameplay loop of TTRPGs: DM narrates, players declare actions, DM narrates consequences, return to start.
The author describes two unfun extremes: a character killed by an illusory scythe trap they couldn't disbelieve, and players repeatedly chanting 'I disbelieve' to slow the game.
The author draws on Blue Bard's 'Death by Illusion' articles, which propose a single save per illusion, where failing means believing it is real.
Under the Blue Bard model, an illusion lasts until it deals damage, then disappears, and the DM checks behind the screen whether characters notice it.
johnbragg on RPG.net proposed distinguishing 'internal' illusions cast directly into someone's mind from 'external' illusions passively encountered with ordinary senses.
The author notes that shapeshifters and doppelgangers are not illusions but still make characters distrust their eyes.
The post lists five illusionist aims: hide a hazard, create a false hazard, delay characters, hide a boon, and create a false boon.
The author's practical split is Active vs Passive illusions, with internal/external mattering mainly for how many people perceive an illusion.
Example from the table: an illusory floor over a real pit is a passive hide-a-hazard illusion, while a bear appearing as a cow is an active one.
The author says illusions are hard to run because they resemble real studies of magic, with arcane cases, means and methods of generating effects.
The author concludes illusions should be used in moderation because their key advantage is surprise, and once folk are alert to them it all comes apart.
The post is labelled blog carnival, D&D, dnd, and worldbuilding on the Seed of Worlds blog by author Xaosseed.
